name: Facial thread lift (cheek lifting)

lead: A thread lift places threads, some with barbs or cones, under the skin to lift the cheeks and midface and soften the nasolabial fold, without removing skin. The lift is visible after the procedure.

The threads anchor and elevate tissue and are placed through small entry points. Wikipedia describes it as a simplified alternative to a facelift. Two trials are registered, one comparing hyaluronic acid-coated and non-coated threads for the midface and one combining threads with microfocused ultrasound; results were not available in the sources reviewed.

paras: It is a short, minimally invasive procedure done in a clinic, with less downtime than surgery. People choose it for a quick midface lift and softer fold lines instead of a facelift.

Physician and media reports describe infection, vessel puncture and pain, and some threads cannot easily be removed. Practitioner training and qualifications vary by country, and complications have drawn media scrutiny.

angle.text: Thread lifts raise the midface and soften the nasolabial fold by hoisting cheek tissue with threads placed under the skin, without removing skin. The lift is visible after the procedure. Efficacy data are limited and mixed, and complications are reported in the literature.

lead: A facial thread lift is a minimally invasive procedure in which thin threads, some barbed or coned, are placed under the skin to raise sagging facial tissue without cutting away skin. For the cheeks, it is used to lift the midface, restore cheek position and soften the nasolabial fold, giving a higher, fuller-looking cheekbone area and a more defined midface.[1][2]

People choose it as a shorter-recovery alternative to a surgical facelift. Surgical rhytidectomy remains the reference procedure for lifting facial tissue and removing excess skin, with costs quoted in the thousands of dollars,[3] while thread lifts are described as a simpler option involving small entry points.[2][4] Some threads are coated with hyaluronic acid, and some practitioners pair them with energy devices such as microfocused ultrasound.[1][5]

Published material on thread lifts consists mainly of registered trials and case reports of complications. A registered trial compared hyaluronic acid-coated and non-coated threads for midface lifting, and another combined threads with microfocused ultrasound; results were not available in the sources reviewed.[1][5] Case reports describe rare complications including a pseudolymphoma, a nerve injury and an artery pseudoaneurysm.[6][7]
infobox: Threads (varied; some barbed, coned or hyaluronic acid-coated)

paras: Thread lifting inserts threads into the subcutaneous layer so that they hold or reposition tissue; the technique is described as simplifying the lifting that a facelift achieves surgically.[2] Threads vary in material and design, and in recent years hyaluronic acid-coated versions have been tested for midface work.[1]
A case report notes that thread lift is also done for jowls and describes it as a blind procedure in which key structures are not directly visualised.[7]

A surgical facelift (rhytidectomy) lifts deeper facial layers and redrapes skin, and it was the third most popular aesthetic surgery in 2019 according to American Society for Aesthetic Plastic Surgery figures cited by Wikipedia.[3] Thread lifting is positioned as a less invasive alternative with a shorter recovery period.[4]

Wikipedia reports that one physician has called it among the riskiest procedures an aesthetic practitioner can perform, noting that some threads stay in the tissue and cannot be pulled out, and that a 2021 BBC investigation of training courses recorded poor infection control and severe patient pain.[2] The article also notes UK aesthetic practitioners needed no mandatory qualifications.[2]

Case reports describe cutaneous pseudolymphoma after a thread lift,[6] glossopharyngeal nerve compression causing hypertension after a jowl-region lift,[7] and a superficial temporal artery pseudoaneurysm two months after a thread lift. Authors of the nerve case note that widespread use has increased the variety and frequency of complications.[7] The pseudolymphoma report lists small bruises, mild redness, transient altered sensation and mild swelling as the comparatively low-incidence usual complications.[6]

A completed 144-participant registered study (NCT07916103, started 2024) compared HA-coated and non-HA threads for midface lifting and nasolabial fold correction.[1] A 45-participant registration (NCT04157218, started 2019, status unknown) examined thread lifting with microfocused ultrasound.[5] No published results were in the sources reviewed. Published literature otherwise consists of complication case reports.[6][7]
